# Reinstalling Battery, Can't Figure Out Where This Cable Goes?

Restoring a motorcycle after long-term storage often involves more than just swapping a cell. When you reinstall a battery on a Suzuki Boulevard C50T and find a loose cable dangling beneath the seat with no obvious termination point, it is easy to assume it was left over from a previous repair or that it belongs to an auxiliary system you aren't familiar with. In this specific scenario, where the fuel injection indicator fails to illuminate immediately after reconnection, identifying that stray wire is critical to restoring electrical continuity.

The cable in question is almost certainly part of the main charging circuit, specifically the ground path for the stator or the primary battery feed before it reaches the fuse box. On many cruiser-style motorcycles like the Boulevard C50T, the battery is often mounted under the seat with the positive terminal accessible but the negative grounding strap routed loosely through the frame tunnels or tucked behind the rear fender. If a user disconnects the battery for transport or storage and then reconnects only the terminals without securing the ground strap, the bike will appear dead.

The fuel injection power light failing to turn on is a classic symptom of an open circuit in the main battery feed. The Electronic Control Unit (ECU) requires stable 12V reference power from the battery to initialize its internal logic and drive the dashboard LEDs. If the ground cable you found is actually the primary negative connection for the stator coil or the main battery negative, leaving it unconnected creates a high-resistance path or an open loop entirely.

To diagnose this without guessing, inspect the frame rails near the engine block. On the Suzuki C50T, the negative battery terminal often connects to a heavy-gauge cable that runs down the side of the frame. Look for a bolted connection point on the engine case or the main chassis rail. If the cable is loose and unconnected, it is likely a ground strap that was dislodged when the seat was removed or the battery was lifted.

Do not attempt to connect this cable to an arbitrary metal surface if it lacks a specific terminal lug. However, you must verify that the negative terminal on the battery itself is securely clamped to its designated post. If the loose cable has no corresponding bolt hole nearby, check the wiring diagram for your specific year model. Sometimes these cables run through the frame and terminate near the rear brake caliper or the ignition switch assembly rather than directly at the battery box.

If you cannot locate a matching connection point after inspecting the chassis, consult the factory service manual for the "Electrical System" section. The wiring diagram will show whether that cable is part of the charging system (stator output) or the battery discharge path. In either case, leaving it unconnected prevents the ECU from receiving the power required to light up the dashboard indicators.

There is a common pitfall when working on storage-restored bikes: assuming all wires are disconnected and safe to ignore once the battery is seated. The reality is that ground straps can shift under their own weight or vibrate loose during transport. Always trace heavy-gauge cables back to their source. If a cable has no connection point, it may be part of a harness that was previously cut for an aftermarket accessory or removed during a prior repair, but it should not be left dangling if the bike is meant to function as a standard issue model.

For those comfortable with diagnostics, you can use a multimeter to check for continuity between the loose cable and the battery negative terminal with the ignition off. If there is continuity and no connection point is visible, you may need to trace the wire along the frame rails until it meets its termination block. Avoid using alligator clips as a permanent solution; soldered or crimped connections on dedicated terminals ensure reliable ground paths that won't corrode or loosen over time.

If you are maintaining a fleet of vehicles and documenting your repairs, consider adding a note to your maintenance log indicating the battery reinstallation date and any ground strap adjustments made. This practice prevents future confusion when returning the bike for service. If you ever encounter a situation where the electrical system behaves erratically after a battery swap, check the ground connections first before investigating fuses or the ECU itself.
